query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys engineered with a bioinspired microstructure, the retention of toughness is primarily governed by the connectivity of an embedded, ductile (plastic) phase. A continuously connected ductile phase network promotes localized plastic deformation (via nanoscale shear band formation) that bridges cracks and deflects crack paths, thereby dissipating fracture energy and retaining toughness. Disrupting this connectivity should lead to a measurable decrease in fracture toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy (or alloy/ceramic hybrid) with a hard matrix and an intentionally engineered, contiguous network of a ductile phase (analogous to the Cr7C3 phase in high‐entropy ceramics).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the volume fraction and spatial connectivity of the ductile phase by altering alloy composition or processing parameters (e.g., heat treatment or additive concentration) while keeping the overall composition nearly constant.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled loading (e.g., standard fracture toughness and flexural strength tests) at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to the service limit, with similar strain rates. The hypothesis is expected to hold in systems designed with a bioinspired, contiguous plastic phase network, but may not apply to alloys with entirely homogeneous or non‐networked microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of connectivity (or network integrity) of the ductile phase dispersed within the hard matrix.
generation.mechanism: A highly interconnected ductile phase enables distributed plasticity through the formation of nanoscale shear bands. This localized plastic deformation absorbs energy and arrests crack propagation via crack bridging and crack deflection. Disruption of the ductile phase connectivity reduces these mechanisms, leading to a more brittle failure and loss of toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a well‐connected ductile phase network will show higher fracture toughness and better retention of strength (compared to a baseline with optimized connectivity), while alloys with a disrupted or less connected ductile phase will exhibit lower fracture toughness and increased brittleness.
generation.baseline: High‐entropy alloy samples with an optimized, contiguous ductile phase network, demonstrating high fracture toughness and strength retention at the tested temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high‐entropy alloys and related ceramic systems that incorporate an engineered ductile phase network. It is expected to be valid within the tested temperature ranges and under controlled strain-rate conditions and may not extend to systems lacking any soft phase or where the ductile phase does not form a connected network.
generation.uncertainty: Although bioinspired ceramic systems (as evidenced by the Cr7C3/HEC materials) support the role of a connected plastic phase in toughening, direct quantitative evidence in high‐entropy alloy systems is still emerging. The precise quantitative relationship between connectivity and toughness retention remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of high‐entropy alloy samples where the volume fraction and connectivity of the ductile phase are systematically varied (e.g., via minor compositional adjustments or postprocessing treatments). Use microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM) to quantify the connectivity of the ductile phase network. Conduct standardized fracture toughness and flexural strength tests on each sample at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Crack path analysis during mechanical loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the data show no significant correlation between the degree of ductile phase connectivity and the measured toughness (i.e., samples with reduced connectivity do not exhibit a consistent reduction in fracture toughness relative to the baseline), then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we realize the design of bioinspired all-ceramics that feature a contiguous network of the Cr7C3 plastic phase uniformly distributed within the predominant HEC [i.e., (Hf, Zr, Ta, Nb, Ti, Cr)C] hard phase, through the high-entropy composition-engineering strategy. Specifically, the resulting HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramics show high KIC of 12.5 ± 1.5 MPa·m1/2 and flexural strength of 613 ± 52 MPa at room temperature (RT), and good strength retention of ~97% up to 1300 °C, surpassing the performance of most other reported bioinspired ceramics. Further in-situ experimental and theoretical investigations provide compelling evidence that the Cr7C3 phase can plastically deform under load, achieving a ~ 30.8% compression strain through forming nanoscale shear bands with significant crystal defects. This plastic deformation behavior, which does not rely on specific crystallographic orientations, effectively enriches the toughening mechanisms in HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramics. Our materials are promising in numerous applications e.g., advanced manufacturing, metallurgy, chemical industry, and aerospace, especially at elevated temperatures.

More importantly, they can retain ~97% of their flexural strength (594 ± 53 MPa) up to 1300 °C, exceeding what could be expected from other bioinspired ceramics. Further in-situ sub-micron pillar compression tests and theoretical calculations confirm that the Cr7C3 phase can accommodate plastic deformation with an engineering strain of ~30.8% by forming multiple nanoscale shear bands, showing ductility that is even comparable to some intermetallic compounds. Such a unique plastic characteristic of Cr7C3 along with its contiguous network distribution results in multiple toughening mechanisms, including crack-bridging by unfractured Cr7C3 ligaments and crack deflection in the HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramics. Our work successfully explores tough and strong bioinspired all-ceramics that can serve up to 1300 °C, providing a strategy to facilitate further design of bioinspired ceramics capable of operating at higher temperatures e.g., substituting Cr7C3 with other plastic high-temperature ceramic phases.

chosen.approach: Bioinspired ceramic design with contiguous plastic phase network
